支聯會及前主席李卓人、前副主席何俊仁、鄒幸彤，被控「煽動顛覆國家政權」罪，支聯會、李卓人、鄒幸彤不認罪，上星期五被裁定罪成。各被告連同早前認罪的何俊仁，今日（28日）求情。鄒幸彤陳詞時，屢次被法官李運騰打斷，其 Patreon 早前上載「我的陳情文」，《集誌社》轉載如下： 相關報道：支聯會案求情．庭外｜排隊黨又亂棄垃圾遭警喝止　「女長毛」被搜身　袋中物品遭逐件拍攝 支聯會案求情．庭內｜鄒幸彤不求情：心安理得，無罪可悔　陳詞屢被法官打斷

鄒幸彤的 Patreon 今日上載其陳情全文。

陳情文 — 鄒幸彤

1. The 206-page judgment, going on and on, essentially says that pursuing democracy is a crime.

2. I do not believe any political party can treat the sovereignty of the state as its private property to give away at will, declaring itself the choice of the people, proclaiming itself the sole leader, and then insisting that every person has a legal duty to uphold this self-appointed throne. Such所谓的 law is nothing but a synonym for tyranny.

3. Believing that authoritarianism is wrong and democracy is right — if this is not conviction, then what is?

4. But the law cannot control anyone's thoughts. Not only can it not, when the law insists on opposing conscience, it is the law that loses, and it is the law alone that forfeits its legitimacy.

5. There must be a bottom line in how one conducts oneself, and the law must have one too. The distinction between democracy and authoritarianism is one of the most important of these bottom lines, because under authoritarianism there can be no rule of law. When the court completely empties out the factual reasons and the moral right and wrong that gave rise to the demand to "end one-party dictatorship," and blindly emphasises only the will of the regime and the so-called duty to obey the law, it is in effect as absurd as saying that those living under Nazi Germany had a duty to exterminate the Jews. Such an approach will only strip the law of its soul of fairness, reducing it to a puppet driven by power.

6. It is precisely this attitude of never questioning right or wrong, of caring only about obedience, that has caused tragedy after tragedy under Nazi rule and under authoritarian rule. The courts today, the state today — they are walking down the same dangerous old path. Moreover, with the progress of technology and the growing power of the state, with the state now recognised as a "great power," the danger today is even greater than in those days.

7. As citizens, we have the responsibility to put the power of the state back behind the bars of democracy, to fulfil our duty as masters of the country by controlling it and overseeing it. To do so is not only to seek justice for the harms of the past, but also to prevent greater disasters from happening again. To fatten, in the name of national security, a state apparatus that we cannot control, one that erodes humanity and conscience, is simply to invite tragedy sooner or later.

8. Therefore, ending one-party dictatorship is an inescapable responsibility for our generation — whether we are Hongkongers or Chinese. This must be done by ourselves, can only be done by ourselves; no one from the outside can do it on our behalf.

9. This is my sincere thought and conviction, and it is by no means mine alone — the candlelight in Victoria Park for thirty years has already proven this. "Ending one-party dictatorship" is the people's bottom line, a universal demand. When the law overreaches and challenges this, it only brings shame upon itself.

10. The court pretends that the issue is not the spreading of ideas but the so-called dissemination of hostility, but the conviction of "ending one-party dictatorship" has never needed to be sustained by any friend-enemy thinking or the stirring up of hatred. We need only reason and facts, and that is enough to win the support of every fair-minded person.

11. Because authoritarianism is itself the greatest, most obvious injustice — it disregards every person's equality and autonomy, forcibly imposes an order of rule that brooks no argument, and degrades free citizens into slaves with no choice. To end one-party dictatorship is simply to fight for the dignity that is due to a human being, and anyone who is not pretending to be asleep should be able to see this clearly.

12. Only those who cannot prevail by reason need to keep mobilising through hatred; we have no need of that. Only those utterly lacking in self-confidence see hostility in everything; we certainly do not see the world that way. We have absolute confidence in what we believe in and what we uphold. Just because dictatorship sustains its rule through hatred does not mean everyone must use its methods, does not mean the world really revolves around hatred. Belief in equality and justice, respect for human nature and truth, have always been stronger and more enduring forces than hatred.

13. Conviction is something that cannot be quantified or traded. To plead, to apologise, for what one believes in is the most hypocritical thing one can do, and it is an insult to all who hold the same belief. So I will not do it, cannot do it — even the executioners of the massacre have not come out to apologise, so how could it be our turn?! Even if the world is turned upside down, we should not apologise for the wrongs done by the regime, lest we ourselves become part of that inversion.

14. As for everything in the past, I refuse to use the language and concepts of crime to analyse how serious or not serious our actions were. If the court really wants some reference, it can ask the Office for Safeguarding National Security led by the Communist Party — they really do know how to look at the struggles for democracy and human rights through the eyes of crime. They have never been shy about saying outright that this case is of a serious nature and must be severely punished, without any sense that they are interfering with judicial independence. In any case, if the court ultimately decides that what we did was "of a serious nature," I will take that as a compliment to us, because it means we really did get something done.

15. Being able to find a mission one believes in, to find companions to fight alongside — that is the most blessed thing in life. So for the path I have walked with the Alliance and with Hongkongers, I have not the slightest regret. I am only sorry for my family and those who love me — they are the only ones to whom I must ask for forgiveness.

16. And as for the future, whether inside or outside prison, I will continue to work, to learn, to better myself, to make all kinds of attempts, for the release of the pro-democracy activists, the vindication of the 1989 pro-democracy movement, the pursuit of accountability for the massacre, the ending of one-party dictatorship, and the building of a democratic Hong Kong and China — until the day democracy arrives. This is a pledge I have made publicly countless times, a solemn vow I made to the dead in the sea of candlelight, and I do not intend to be a man without honour.

17. If doing so makes me a permanent criminal, if the law truly cannot accommodate our convictions, then I would rather be a criminal than a traitor to my conscience. I will walk this unfinished road to democracy together with all Hongkongers who refuse to accept their fate.

18.　　The candlelight is a sea; the hearts of the people become waves; broken bodies beat against the shore; injustice will never rest.
